newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia questions Soros Foundation chief.
newsitem.headline: Croatia questions Soros Foundation chief.

text.p: Croatian police on Friday detained a senior official of the U.S.-based Soros Foundation, which promotes democracy in Eastern Europe, but released her after questioning, Foundation staff said.

Karmen Basic, executive director of the Soros Open Society office in Zagreb was released after two hours. Police also released two of her associates who spent the night in custody after being detained on Thursday at a border crossing with Slovenia. Customs confiscated $65,000 in cash from them.

"We spent 21 hours at the department for suppression of commercial crime. We were released with no charges brought against us," said Srdjan Dvornik, managing director of the Soros foundation in Zagreb.
The person detained with him was Ivanka Marton, the foundation's accountant.
The money was not returned and no comment was available from police.
State television said customs found the money in a private car in which Dvornik and Marton were travelling.
"As they didn't report the money to the customs legal proceedings will be initiated and the sum will most probably be confiscated," the television said.
It claimed customs officials discovered a "secret channel for smuggling foreign currency into Croatia for financing Soros activities".
But a Finance Ministry official told Reuters that travellers entering Croatia were not normally required to report foreign currency on their person.
"I saw no reason to presume it was not permitted (to bring in foreign currency)," Dvornik said.

The crackdown on the foundation, which promotes free media and cultural projects to foster democracy in Eastern Europe, came days after President Franjo Tudjman called it an enemy of Croatia's independence.

Speaking at the annual congress of his nationalist HDZ party last week, Tudjman said the foundation, set up by Hungarian-born U.S. fund manager George Soros, had "infiltrated" Croatian society, particularly culture and media.

He accused Soros, "other American and European foundations" and some Western embassies in Croatia of supporting his domestic opposition, helping several small magazines and systematically enlarging the scope of their activities.

"With Soros' help they have infiltrated the entire society. They grant scholarships to all sorts of people and all generations... and they clearly state their aim is to change the ownership structure of the media," Tudjman said.
The foundation finances several media and cultural projects to promote democracy in Eastern Europe.
Since 1993 the Open Society had donated some $15 million to Croatia in various forms.

It was banned in Serbian-led Yugoslavia, from which Croatia seceded in 1991, for a few months earlier this year. But a foundation official said he did not expect quite such severe measures to be applied in Croatia.
"It is just harassment, I don't think they are going to ban us," a foundation source said.
